vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair across from the therapist's desk, his leg bouncing with a restless energy that seems to have become permanent. At twenty-eight, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone who has learned to take up less space, though his broad shoulders and the way his jaw tightens suggest he wasn't always this way.

Three years ago, Marcus was serving as a communications specialist with a NATO contingent in Afghanistan. He was good at his job—translating, coordinating media relations, the kind of work that felt meaningful. On a Tuesday morning in spring, his convoy was traveling to a meeting with local officials when the IED detonated. The blast came from nowhere and everywhere at once. Marcus remembers the sound first, a pressure that seemed to come from inside his own chest. Then the confusion—the acrid smell, the ringing in his ears that wouldn't stop, the weight of debris across his legs. His colleague Dmitri, who had been sitting beside him, was gone. Just gone.

He was evacuated within hours, treated for shrapnel wounds and a fractured tibia. The physical injuries healed relatively quickly. The other injuries didn't.

Marcus returned to civilian life eighteen months ago. He moved in with his girlfriend, Sophie, and took a job as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm. On paper, it seemed like the right move—creative work, flexible hours, far removed from anything that could hurt him. But the transition has been harder than anyone anticipated, and lately, Sophie has started asking questions he can't quite answer.

The hypervigilance is the first thing he notices each day. When he wakes, there's a moment—sometimes just a second, sometimes longer—where he doesn't remember where he is. His heart races. Sophie has learned not to touch him without warning. Three weeks ago, she reached over to adjust his pillow while he was sleeping, and he nearly threw her across the bed. He apologized for hours, but the shame lingers.

At work, the open office environment feels suffocating. He sits with his back to the wall, always aware of exits, always tracking who moves behind him. His manager has commented that he seems tense, that he needs to "relax a bit." Marcus has started taking longer lunch breaks, eating alone in his car in the parking lot, where he can see everything. He's good at his job—content calendars, engagement metrics, brand voice—but he finds himself unable to concentrate. When he's supposed to be crafting a post about a client's new product line, his mind is somewhere else entirely. The constant notifications on his phone feel like threats. Every ping makes him flinch.

The nightmares come three or four times a week. Sometimes he's back in the convoy. Sometimes Dmitri is alive, and Marcus has to watch him die over and over. Other nights, he dreams that the blast followed him home, that it's coming for Sophie. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and often lies awake for the rest of the night rather than risk falling back asleep.

Sophie loves him—he knows this—but he can feel her pulling away. She wants to plan a vacation, to go out with friends, to talk about the future. Marcus wants these things too, but wanting them and being able to do them are different things entirely. He's irritable in ways he doesn't mean to be. Last week, she mentioned that she'd been thinking about marriage, and he snapped at her so harshly that she left the room in tears. He didn't even understand why he was angry.

The weight of existing in the world has become exhausting. He's here, physically present, doing the things that people do. But there's a distance between Marcus and everything else now—a thick, invisible barrier that makes even the people he loves feel unreachable.
